summary: This document describes a message encryption scheme for the Web Push protocol. It gives confidentiality and integrity for messages sent from an application server to a user agent, so the push service that carries them cannot read them.

eli5.summary: Notifications travel through a middleman. This puts them in a sealed box, so the middleman delivers it but cannot open it.

subtitle: How Web Push messages are encrypted end to end so the push service cannot read or forge them.

tldr.problem: Web Push messages travel from an application server to a user agent through a push service, which could otherwise inspect, modify or forge them.
tldr.mechanism: The user agent and application server use ECDH on the P-256 curve plus a 16-octet authentication secret, derive keys with HKDF and SHA-256, and encrypt with the aes128gcm content coding from RFC 8188 in a single record.
tldr.outcome: The push service still sees who talks to whom, when, and how long messages are, but it cannot read or forge the content.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Web Push protocol (RFC 8030) is intermediated by necessity. Messages from an application server reach a user agent (UA) through a push service. This RFC describes how those messages can be secured against inspection, modification and forgery by the push service.

Push messages are the payload of an HTTP message and are encrypted with the encrypted content encoding of RFC 8188. This document says how that encoding is applied and describes a recommended key management scheme.

A central agent at the user agent, such as a web browser implementing the Push API, can enforce the scheme by forwarding only messages that were properly encrypted.
sections.eli5: A message goes from a sender to your phone through a post office. This RFC puts the message in a locked box so the post office only carries it.

sections.title: The Encryption Overview
sections.content:
Encryption uses Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) on the P-256 curve to establish a shared secret, plus a symmetric secret for authentication.

For each subscription it creates, the user agent generates an ECDH key pair and an authentication secret. The public key and the authentication secret are sent to the application server with the other subscription details.

When sending a message, the application server generates its own ECDH key pair and a random salt. Its public key goes in the keyid parameter of the content coding header and the salt in the salt parameter. The key pair can be discarded after encrypting the message.
sections.eli5: Each side makes a pair of keys, shares one half, and mixes the halves to get a secret only the two of them know.

sections.title: Distributing the Keys
sections.content:
The application that owns the subscription passes the subscription public key and authentication secret to an authorized application server, possibly together with the push subscription URI.

It MUST use an authenticated, confidentiality-protected channel. If the authentication secret leaked, unauthorized parties could generate push messages that the user agent would accept. Most applications already have a relationship with their application server, and a mechanism such as HTTPS is sufficient.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake has to be passed along privately, or anyone could pretend to be the sender.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Encryption
sections.content:
Encryption happens in four phases: derive an ECDH shared secret, combine it with the authentication secret to make the input keying material (IKM), derive a content encryption key and nonce as in RFC 8188, then encrypt or decrypt.

The user agent MUST generate a hard-to-guess 16-octet authentication secret, and SHOULD use a cryptographically strong random number generator. The combining step uses HKDF with SHA-256 and these inputs:

  • salt: the authentication secret.
  • IKM: the ECDH shared secret.
  • info: the string WebPush: info, a zero octet, the user agent public key and the application server public key, both in uncompressed point form.
  • L: 32 octets.

The RFC then gives the full sequence in pseudocode. The content encryption key is the first 16 octets of an HMAC-SHA-256 output, and the nonce is the first 12. The exclusive-OR of the nonce with the record sequence number is omitted because a push message has only one record, with sequence number zero.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix the shared secret with a private password and a random pinch of salt, then cook that down into the exact key and starting number the lock needs.

sections.title: Restrictions on aes128gcm
sections.content:
To keep receivers simple, the RFC narrows how the aes128gcm content coding may be used.

  • An application server MUST encrypt a push message as a single record and MUST set rs larger than the plaintext, the 1-octet padding delimiter, any padding and the 16-octet authentication tag.
  • The keyid MUST hold the application server public key: 65 octets in uncompressed form, starting with 0x04.
  • A push service need not support more than 4096 octets of payload. After the 86-octet header, at least 1 octet of padding and 16 octets of expansion, that leaves at most 3993 octets of plaintext.
  • No other content encodings MAY be used, because compression could leak message contents. Content-Encoding has exactly one value, aes128gcm.

A user agent MAY ignore rs and need not support multiple records. It MUST check the padding delimiter octet, and a value other than 0x02 MUST cause the message to be discarded.
sections.eli5: Each message must fit in exactly one box, use one kind of lock, and end with a check mark. If the check mark is wrong, the receiver throws the message away.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows an HTTP POST to a push service with TTL: 10, Content-Length: 145 and Content-Encoding: aes128gcm. The body is the base64url-encoded header and ciphertext. The plaintext is the ASCII string "When I grow up, I want to be a watermelon".

It lists the authentication secret, and the private and public keys for both the receiver and the sender. Appendix A gives every intermediate value: the shared secret, the key-combining values, the content encryption key, the nonce, and the 86-octet header. Implementers can use these to check their own code.
sections.eli5: The RFC includes a full answer key, so builders can check that their lock and key produce the same result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 8030 and the limits of RFC 8188 apply. No HTTP header fields are protected by the content encoding, so a user agent MUST treat header fields as coming from the push service. An application that changes its behavior based on those fields is exposed to attack by the push service.

Timing and message length cannot be hidden from the push service, which sees which application server talks to which user agent on which subscription. Length can be hidden only by using the padding that the content encoding provides.

The user agent and application MUST verify that any public key they receive is on the P-256 curve. Skipping that check can let an attacker extract a private key. The validation has three steps: check the point is not the point at infinity, check both integers are in the correct interval, and check the point solves the curve equation.

If the scheme ever needs replacing, a new content coding could be defined, and the user agent could advertise which codings it supports.
sections.eli5: The middleman cannot read the box but can see who sends boxes to whom and how big they are, and you must check that a key is real before using it.
